A Tool Library for the Neighborhood

Last year, our community center opened a small tool library. The idea grew from a simple observation: many households own drills, ladders, or saws that they use only a few times a year. Instead of asking every family to buy the same equipment, the center invited residents to donate safe tools they no longer needed. Each item is checked before it -------(25)------- on the shelves. Volunteers also keep a repair log so that damaged items are not accidentally put back -------(27)------- circulation. When a tool cannot be fixed, useful parts are removed before the rest is recycled. The center does not claim that sharing is always -------(28)------- than owning. A person who uses the same tool every week may still prefer to buy one. -------(29)-------, for occasional jobs, borrowing can reduce both cost and clutter. groups.instructions: Read the report about mapping heat on a school campus and answer the questions.
groups.passage:
Mapping Heat on a School Campus

A group of students wanted to understand why some parts of their school grounds felt much hotter than others. Rather than relying on impressions alone, they borrowed simple digital thermometers and measured surface temperatures at the same six locations for two weeks. Measurements were taken shortly after noon on dry days. The students recorded whether each location was shaded, the kind of surface beneath the thermometer, and whether a breeze was noticeable.

The results did not produce a neat ranking every day. A concrete wall that was extremely warm on one afternoon was cooler after clouds arrived the next day. Even so, two patterns appeared repeatedly. Dark paving tended to be warmer than grass, and shaded benches were usually cooler than nearby benches in direct sun. The group therefore proposed planting two small trees near the hottest waiting area.

Their science teacher supported the proposal but warned against treating the study as proof that trees alone would solve the problem. The measurements covered only a short period, and the group had not measured air temperature or humidity. The students responded by describing their work as a “first map” rather than a final answer. They also suggested repeating the survey in another season before deciding where additional shade would have the greatest effect.

questions.question_text: What was the students’ main purpose in collecting measurements?

options.text: To prove that every concrete surface is unsafe
To calculate the school’s monthly electricity use
To decide which students should work outdoors
To compare heat conditions at several places on the campus

options.text: To determine how quickly each surface cooled after sunset
To compare how much rainfall each surface received
To make the observations more comparable

questions.question_text: Which factor was NOT recorded by the students?
The phrase “a neat ranking” most nearly means -------.

options.text: a colorful map of the school grounds
a consistent order from hottest to coolest
a list arranged by student preference

questions.question_text: What pattern appeared repeatedly in the data?

options.text: Cloudy days made every location equally warm.
Concrete walls were always the hottest surfaces.
Breezy locations were never in direct sunlight.
Dark paving was often warmer than grass.

questions.question_text: Why did the teacher hesitate to call the study conclusive?

options.text: The thermometers were too expensive to use again.
It covered limited conditions and omitted some measurements.
The students had measured only indoor locations.
No student had written down the surface types.

questions.question_text: What can be inferred from the students calling their work a “first map”?

options.text: They recognized that more evidence was needed.
They planned to stop collecting data permanently.
They believed the tree proposal had already failed.

questions.question_text: Which action would best extend the study as the students proposed?

options.text: Paint every path before collecting more data.

groups.instructions: Read the article about community repair events and answer the questions.
groups.passage:
Why Repair Events Teach More Than Repair

Once a month, a community hall in a small town fills with broken lamps, loose chair legs, silent radios, and people who hope these objects can be used again. The event is organized as a repair afternoon. Visitors bring one item and sit beside a volunteer who has experience with tools, sewing, or basic electronics. The volunteer does not simply take the object away and return it later. Whenever possible, the owner stays at the table, watches the diagnosis, and performs a safe part of the repair.

This arrangement makes the event slower than a commercial repair service, but speed is not its main measure of success. Organizers want participants to leave with a clearer idea of how everyday objects are put together. A visitor who learns how to tighten a loose connection may later inspect another device before deciding to replace it. Even when an item cannot be saved, opening it carefully can reveal why it failed and which materials can be separated for recycling.

The events also create an unusual form of conversation. People who might never meet elsewhere compare practical knowledge across generations. An older volunteer may know how to mend a wooden drawer, while a teenager may be more comfortable finding a digital manual. Neither kind of knowledge is treated as automatically superior. Instead, the useful question is which approach fits the problem on the table.

There are limits. Volunteers refuse repairs that involve serious electrical danger or equipment requiring licensed specialists. They also avoid promising that every repaired object will last indefinitely. These boundaries matter because enthusiasm can create false confidence. A safe repair culture depends on knowing when to stop as well as knowing how to begin.

For the organizers, the strongest evidence of success is therefore not a pile of rescued objects. It is the moment when a visitor asks a better question about an object, uses a tool with more care, or explains a newly learned step to someone else. In that sense, repair is both a practical activity and a way of making technical knowledge less mysterious.
